topic: restoring a shepherd's hut: rotten floor bearers, the stove flue and moving it on its old axles

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-5)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: cyfrowa waga pod osiami

base: I am restoring an old shepherd's hut and the floor has rotted along one side.
The small stove inside is original and still draws well once the flue warms up.
A digital axle scale sits under each wheel and shows how the weight is spread.
The rot runs from the door corner back about four feet along the bearer.
Should I patch that corner, or lift the whole floor and start again?
Lift the whole floor, because rot in a bearer never stops where you can see it.
The bearers carry everything, and a patched one will drop again within two winters.
Take the boards up whole where you can, since old floorboards are worth relaying.
Look hard at the chassis timbers underneath before you order any new stock.
I lifted the floor and found the door side bearer soft for its whole length.
The axle scale reads three hundred kilos on that side and two forty on the other.
The small stove stands on the heavy side, which may explain some of the difference.
Is that much difference a worry, or do these huts always sit unevenly?
Sixty kilos across a hut of that size is ordinary and nothing to correct.
The stove, the water can and the bunk were always set to one side.
What matters is that both axles carry their share when the hut stands level.
Replace the soft bearer in oak and bed it on the iron chassis with felt.
The new oak bearer is in and the floorboards went back with only three replaced.
The axle scale now shows the two sides within twenty kilos of each other.
The small stove is back on its plate, though the flue leaks smoke at the collar.
Should I seal that collar with rope and cement, or fit a new one?
Fit a new collar, since rope and cement will crack again by the second winter.
A leaking collar drives smoke into the roof space where you will never see it.
Set the new one on fire cement while the stove is cold and leave it a week.
Check the roof sheet around the collar too, because rain follows the same path down.
The new collar went on and the smoke now goes straight up the flue.
The roof sheet around it had rusted through in two places, exactly as you said.
I patched the sheet, but the whole roof is thin and rattles in any wind.
Is a whole new roof worth it, or will patching see the hut through?
A new roof is worth it, because everything below a leaking roof rots in turn.
Corrugated sheet is cheap and a hut of this size takes very few lengths.
Keep the old sheets for the sides, where they still have years of life.
Fix the new sheet with hook bolts and wool washers rather than nails.
The new sheets are on with hook bolts and the roof has stopped rattling entirely.
The hut feels sound now and stands square when I lower it onto its wheels.
I would like to move it two fields over before the ground turns soft.
Can it be towed slowly behind a tractor, or is that asking for trouble?
Tow it slowly, at walking pace, and only over ground that is firm throughout.
The old axles run on plain bearings and will heat badly at any real speed.
Grease them the day before and feel the hubs after the first few hundred yards.
Chock the wheels as soon as it stands, since these huts run away on a slope.
